speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Inasmuch as negotiations on the content of the proposed Canada Health Act between the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the provincial Ministers of Health have broken down, and the Minister is now going to recommend unilateral action to the Cabinet, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway):
That this House call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in the spirit of co-operative federalism, to re-open negotiations with the provincial Ministers of Health on the subject of the Canada Health Act.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my motion under Standing Order 43 deals with a most serious accusation of alleged irregularities within the Canadian Dairy Commission which has prompted an inquiry by the RCMP. The CDC currently has liabilities of $287.7 million from a drawing account of $300 million, and it annually collects millions in special levies against dairy producers. In view of this RCMP investigation and of the appearance, as witnesses, of senior officials of CDC before the Public Accounts Committee, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That, until the Canadian Dairy Commission is out from under the dark cloud hovering over it, direction of its day-to-day operations be removed from the Minister, and its Chairman, and placed under trusteeship to protect the huge
financial investment of the federal Government and the Financial contributions of dairy producers across Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is directed to

November 15, 1982
Oral Questions
the Minister of Finance. It concerns the Royal Commission that has been established by the Prime Minister in connection with Canada's economic union and future economic course. In the press release issued by the Prime Minister to announce this Royal Commission, he said that the terms of reference of the Commission are "perhaps the most important and far-reaching that have ever been assigned to any commission" in this country. We have been awaiting the announcement of the composition of this Commission, which was to come within ten days of the announcement of the appointment of the Commission itself on November 5.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance if he is now in a position to tell who the other members of this Commission are, or has he not been advised of this? Has he not received any word from Senator Keith Davey or Jim Coutts on who will be the other members of this Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, consultations are practically completed. The announcement should be made soon, but certainly not before the return of the Prime Minister, since the Commission itself, appointed by the Cabinet of Canada, is appointed upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister.

Having spent some days in his constituency during the past short recess, Madam Speaker, the Minister will know that one of the major concerns about the Commission is the question of credibility. It is perceived to be a partisan, political Commission headed by a man who seeks the Liberal leadership.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the terms of reference provide that the Commission will look into the appropriate national goals and policies for economic development of our country. Mr. Macdonald is a director of a number of multinational corporations and large Canadian corporations which include Boise Cascade Corp. Ltd., McDonnell Douglas Corp. Ltd., the Bank of Nova Scotia, and other corporations. In order that there will be no perception of conflict of interest in the carrying out of his responsibilities, will the Minister of Finance obtain from Mr. Macdonald his undertaking to resign from these corporate boards, in order for him to be perceived as being independent in his assessments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I hope when the names of the Commissioners are announced and the Hon. Member sees a few well-known Canadians with strong Conservative affiliations that he will not conclude they have immediate leadership ambitions in the Conservative Party.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can assure him that the Hon. Member for St. John's West is not on that list, however.
That's a relief!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: As far as the question itself is concerned, surely my friend should rejoice over the fact that we have a man to head this Commission who has extensive experience, not only in public administration but also one with a good knowledge of the private sector of the Canadian economy. As far as the directorships are concerned, I will certainly raise the issue with the Prime Minister when he returns so that he can raise it with Mr. Macdonald.
Unlike the Hon. Minister of Finance, we on this side of the House are not desperate for new leadership in our Party.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!
The Liberals can take this matter as humorous, the economic future of the country, but it is most serious.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there were reports over the weekend on the 40 per cent increase in bankruptcies in the country and unprecedented unemployment, with more people on the dole this winter season than ever before in the history of Canada. To use a well-known Conservative statement, the people of Canada do not want to wait for spring; they want to do it now, and they want the Government to do it now.
Will any of the results or recommendations of the Commission be available to the Government before the end of the term of inquiry, that is, three years, because it is apparent to me that the Government is completely bankrupt of any new ideas in terms of economic direction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I never said that the Conservatives were desperate about their leadership. I only implied that they were terribly scared, and from listening to the Hon. Member this is what I would have to conclude.
I want to tell him that the Royal Commission itself will examine the immediate and long-term prospects of the Canadian economic union. The Government is not waiting for the report of that Commission before taking action to deal with the very serious recession we are experiencing at the present time. The Commission is no substitute for decisions which will have an immediate impact.
I announced a number of decisions in my economic statement of October 27, and subsequently the Minister of Employment and Immigration arrived at agreements with the provinces whereby the provinces will add certainly well over $100 million to the $500 million we are putting into direct job creation. The Hon. Member also knows about the $1.5 billion
November 15, 1982

of direct and indirect job creation which we have in operation at the present time.
The Government is taking appropriate steps; there will be more steps taken in the months to come. The Royal Commission will examine the future of Canada in terms of the economic union and of the future prosperity of the country over the next two decades.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. In accepting the chairmanship of the Commission, Donald Macdonald specifically stated that, with the Government's agreement, the option was open to him to resign and run for the leadership of the Liberal Party. In that event, my question is twofold. First, if this is the most important and far reaching Commission in the history of the country, do the people of Canada not have the right to expect that its Chairman will stay and finish the job? Second, how can the Chairman be properly critical of present and past government policies when such criticism would erode confidence in the party which he hopes to lead, and irritate delegates he hopes to attract?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have already indicated to the Hon. Member that I was not aware of any decision to the effect that Mr. Macdonald would not conclude the work of the Commission. I hope this Commission will work speedily and effectively and bring forward a report that will be of benefit to the whole of Canada.
Second, this Commission is not going to spend its time examining the last 50 years. I hope it will spend its time examining the next 20 to 30 years, that it will provide Canada with the framework and plans for action that will be of benefit to the whole of Canada-
Self-sufficiency by 2020-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: -and that will bring about a better economic union in this country and better prosperity for all Canadians.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance who indicated in a previous answer that he seems to know who the members of this Commission are going to be. I ask the Minister whether or not Ian Stewart is going to be a member of this Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 am not in a position to tell the Hon. Member what the exact composition of the Commission will be.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Just answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As I indicated, the Prime Minister will make recommendations to Cabinet on his return after the consultations have been concluded.

speakerposition: subtopic
N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Minister is no doubt aware that, through a series of transactions during the course of the last week, some hundreds of millions of dollars changed hands in Toronto. The end result is that approximately 10 per cent of the rental units available in that city are now owned, or will shortly be owned, by Saudi Arabian investors.
It is very difficult to see what significant benefit will flow to Canada from this takeover. I have looked at all of the criteria set out under FIRA, and I cannot find a single criterion under which this particular transaction will provide a benefit and therefore qualify. Will the Minister order that this transaction be stopped until such time as FIRA has an opportunity to review it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
1
agree with the Hon. Member, Madam Speaker, if the allegations are proved to be correct, as reported in the media this past week, with respect to this transaction or series of transactions. I can tell the Hon. Member at this time that my officials are looking into the situation to see if this case can be reviewed under FIRA.

speakerposition: subtopic
N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is quite clear that the transaction is the takeover of a business operating in Canada that provides not only a profit for those who own the shares but also accommodation for tens of thousands of Canadians, many of whom cannot afford to absorb the cost that will be passed through to them as a result of this transaction. What possible question could there be as to whether or not this transaction falls under the terms that caused FIRA to be set up to protect Canadians from unfair takeovers of Canadian industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, counsel for some of the participants in the transaction advised us that this transaction was not reviewable under the Act. Consequently, the Minister, under Section 8 of the Act, as I recall, has the power to have the case reviewed if he finds reasonable and probable grounds to have it reviewed. This is a very complex situation and that is why our officials are taking the time, together with officials of the Department of Justice, to look into the situation.

November 15, 1982
OraI Questions

speakerposition: subtopic
N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I go back to the Minister again because it is clear, on the face of it, that there will be significant numbers of Canadians who will be asked to absorb what is now quite clearly an inflated price, the result of some backroom shenanigans undertaken by persons who have for years represented the Tory Party in Ontario.
Oh, oh!
That is why they are not asking any questions.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Quite pointedly, in order to assure that those tenants will not be forced to carry that burden, and in order to assure that this kind of thing will not be allowed to happen in other centres in Canada-in Vancouver, in Hamilton, in Montreal and in Ottawa-will the Minister step in and say that this transaction cannot be completed until he has reviewed it? And, upon review, if the facts are borne out as they are presented today, will the Minister stop it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Multicul-turalism. On November 2 he condemned outright a list of ethnic groups and leaders that was drawn up by the Government of Quebec. He said flatly that the Government of Canada would not engage in such activity. My question, however, arises from a 1974 document called "A Revised Handbook of Selected Ethnic Organizations in Canada", of which I understand the Minister is aware. It contains profiles of a number of ethnic organizations in Canada and, in some cases, it mentions ethnic leaders. In many cases the descriptions are very unflattering, accusing them of being neo-Nazi, of being communist, of being racist, of being extremist, and so on.
Why was this document drawn up? Why was it strictly confidential? For what purpose was it used? Will the minister undertake to have this document released so that groups and individuals who were profiled in it will see how they are viewed by the Government of Canada and will have a chance to respond to the very serious allegations that are made in it?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I said at the time I was questioned by, I believe, the Hon. Member for Saint Denis, I had checked with my officials. There was no comparable list to the list put out by the Quebec Minister of Cultural Affairs. That list gave political affiliation in domestic terms, political biases or slants. In some cases it listed criminal backgrounds or activities.
A newsman and a newswoman came to me in the past seven days and brought to my attention a book which was last produced in 1974, that listed organizations, the purpose of the organizations, and a definition of the political goals in the sense of old country politics. The officials who lead my directorate, and I, have been unaware of the book. It has not been in circulation or used, to the best of my knowledge or their knowledge, since 1974. I can hardly answer questions by the Hon. Member on why it was done at that time, except, that upon asking my officials if they could recall-because they did not know of the existence of the book-the explanation given was that, as the multiculturalism directorate focused with the Minister of State, it was important, when people or organizations came forward for funding, to know what the goals of those organizations were. Incidentally, I have ordered the book destroyed although it was quite different from the list prepared in Quebec, as I tried to point out earlier, and my previous answer is quite consistent with my answer today.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with your permission, on behalf of the Government of Canada I would like to rise on a point of order to place on record our feelings at the news of the death over the weekend of the former Lieutenant-Governor of the Province of Quebec, the Hon. Hugues Lapointe.

I am very proud, and I trust the House will allow me a few minutes, to pay tribute to a man who served his country with great distinction in a number of impressive functions. His military career, like that of thousands of other Canadians-he served overseas with the Chaudiere Regiment-was a symbol of the great respect he had for traditional values, and he was driven by the will to defend the rights and freedoms Canadians have acquired in the course of our short but eventful history. As a young man, he saw politics as a challenge and never hesitated to defend his ideals. He was a worthy representative of all Canadians and was proud to represent his fellow Canadians from Quebec. In his riding of Lotbiniere, he was both respected and loved for his innate understanding of the democratic way of doing things and for his readiness to share in the joys and sorrows, the successes and disappointments of others. He served with valor as a soldier and with integrity as an elected representative. He was a competent minister and a Canadian in every sense of the word, at all times.
We shall remember him as we remember so many other Canadians who never lost confidence in the future of this great country and thought it worthwhile to defend it in every way.

To his family and friends, on behalf of all Quebecers and all Canadians, I extend the heartfelt wishes of this House. Hugues Lapointe will be greatly missed.

That this House condemns the Government for its failure to introduce its promised comprehensive industrial strategy to rebuild the Canadian economy in the 1980's and for its failure to produce specific strategies to harness the potential of Canadian industry, to promote the advantageous utilization of Canada's human and natural resources, to increase exports of Canadian manufactured goods, and to provide incentives for training opportunities and to the private sector for new, and increased levels of research and development in Canada.
He said: Madam Speaker, in rising to speak to the motion now before the House, I do so with an unexpected assist from today's Globe and Mail which has extensive references to this subject. I refer, of course, to the fact that we find a leaked story on page B1 of The Globe and Mail setting out that: "Industrial strategy begins with talks".
I mention this because I think it is interesting that the first point we make in our motion is to condemn the Government for its failure to introduce its promised comprehensive industrial strategy to rebuild the Canadian economy in the 1980s. We are dead on, Mr. Speaker, because here we have a report in today's Globe and Mail setting out that the talks with respect to an industrial strategy are going to begin in November, 1982 at a time when there is no one in this country with any uncertainty in their minds concerning the inadequancy of this Government's programs to get our country prosperous again. In short, I am saying that this motion, on its first point, has to be one which most Members of this House will agree with because this Government has no industrial strategy, by its own admission. In fact, if one believes the report in The Globe and Mail, the Government is only beginning to talk today about an industrial strategy for the 1980s, notwithstanding the fact that almost 20 per cent of this decade is already behind us.
In our motion today, Mr. Speaker, I think you will find that certainly myself and most of our speakers are going to dwell on the positive aspects of what can be done to get Canada moving
Supply
once again. I say that because I think most Canadians feel a great sense of frustration with the fact that they know we can do better, but they sense, for reasons they cannot clearly perceive, that we are failing to increase our national wealth, the real growth of our economy, that in fact we are poorer today on an average basis than we were six or seven years ago.
I dwell on that, Mr. Speaker, because I think we must never forget that Canadians are a very inventive people. Historically we have shown that, given the proper atmosphere, the proper break if you like, we can be among the world's leaders in inventions.
On that point, if I may, I would like to just remind Members of some of the things which have been invented in Canada. For example, back in 1857 James Miller Williams brought in the first commercial oil well in North America at Oil Springs near Sarnia. I was thinking just last week, when that fact was drawn to my attention once again, what a strange transition we have here. In the last century, in 1857, Canada was a pioneer in bringing in commercial oil wells in North America. A Canadian was the first.
Today we have a Government which devotes its efforts in the oil and gas field to bringing in a National Energy Program which is generally credited with hamstringing that industry in this country. Not only has the Government brought in such a program to hamstring other sectors of the energy field, but it has, of course, introduced us to a thing called Petro-Canada. That company has now cost us some $3 billion, Mr. Speaker. I am going to touch on that later because I would like us all to consider what that S3 billion could have been used for other than simply buying out the oil and gas interests of foreign concerns in Canada, a buy-out which did not create one more barrel of oil, one new invention, or add one nickel to the wealth of this country.
Let me go on, though, to touch on some of the great inventions which Canada has had over the years. 1 do not have to remind the House that 1874 was the year Dr. Alexander Graham Bell invented the principle of the telephone in Brantford, Ontario, and we now find that Canada in truth is one of the pioneers with regard to communication, especially telephone communication, around the world. In 1884, almost 100 years ago, we find that Sir Sandford Fleming invented standard time. It was subsequently adopted by all the railways in North America and became the standard around the world as far as timekeeping is concerned. In 1887 we have Sir William Osier, who at the age of 39 was chosen to head the medical school at the newly-formed John Hopkins University in the United States. He is generally credited with having revolution-alized the treatment of patients in hospitals, not just in Canada or North America, but throughout the world. Given the chance, Mr. Speaker, this is the type of innovative and inventive person we have had in Canada over the decades Canada has been in existence.

November 15, 1982
Supply
As you know, three types of sports all began or were invented in Canada. Basketball, football and hockey all started in this country. We find, for example, that Sir Frederick Banting, who discovered the beneficial effects of insulin on diabetes, was given a Nobel prize for his invention and was also generally regarded as one of the greatest medical achievers of our century. Sir Charles Saunders, back in 1904, developed the Marquis strain of wheat, and later developed the Ruby, Garnet and Reward strains of wheat which were very suitable to Canadian prairie conditions. On his death a London newspaper said that he contributed more to the wealth of this country than any other man.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we have a list of people who in past years have been inventive, who have brought, if you like, real wealth to Canada, second to none in the world. Then, Mr. Speaker, at a time when the world economy is still flourishing, still prospering, why do we find that we are lagging? Why has the spark for research and development in this country started to lag? Why do we now find that, rather than keeping up with world trade, we are falling behind?
There may be some on the Government side who will say "Show us why we are falling behind". In anticipation of that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer them to the fourth Report of the Special Committee on the National Trading Corporation which was presented to this House and sets out the exact position that Canada is in today with respect to world trade. I mention this because I think it is interesting to read the morning press and find that we are still talking about having further discussions concerning what we might do to turn trade around to our advantage in Canada.
The time for talking has ended. We know what the problems are and we know what some of the solutions are. It is time for the Government to have the courage to put in place a program that will start rebuilding Canada, especially with respect to our manufacturing and trade position for the 1980s. I say this because the Special Committee stated that it met with 450 witnesses in Canada and nine other countries. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it heard from people in ten countries, including Canada. It held 270 meetings. It presented an extensive report that, first of all, dramatizes what it believes is the true nature of our deficit in world trade and then it offers solutions.
With that kind of background-the background that I will refer to shortly that the Science Council of Canada has been giving to the Government day after day and year after year- why does the Government have to tell us it is still time to have discussions and hear from more people? It is time for decision, Mr. Speaker. We do not need more discussion and bafflegab from the Government.
On page 3 of its report the Special Committee stated:
-trade deficit in the end product category, which in 1980 accounted for a staggering trade imbalance of $18 billion.
It goes on to point out that the share of total world trade Canada enjoyed in 1972 was 4.9 per cent and that by 1980 that percentage had fallen to 3.2 per cent.
I would remind Hon. Members that this is not some outside think-tank group which is speculating about the facts; it is a
Special Committee of this House that pointed out that our trade in manufactured products has fallen so far behind that we now have a deficit of $18 billion, and only 3.2 per cent of total world trade compared to 4.9 per cent in 1972.
On page 5 the report goes on to say:
Between 1969 and 1979 Canada suffered a 33 per cent decline in its overall share of world exports. This performance was the worst among industrialized countries during this period. Nor do we fare any better in comparisons with the major developing countries. In the period 1969-79, Canada's average annual export growth rate was 15.1 per cent; the developing countries averaged 23.1 per cent. Canada pays a very high price for this lost market share-a price that this country can no longer afford.
The report goes on to mention that if one uses the assumptions it has been able to come up with in its research data, $8 billion to $12 billion of opportunity in additional exports is being lost to Canadians at the present time. It also points out that if foreign sales could be improved by only 10 per cent on average, that would mean Canadians would have an additional $6 billion in sales of manufactured goods, creating new customers around the world. But here is the crunch, Mr. Speaker. Having demonstrated the imbalance, especially in end-products trade, the report goes on to say:
Exports also have the potential to increase employment. At present, small and medium business account for 70 per cent of all manufacturing jobs; efforts that result in more sales will add impressively to employment totals. Committee research indicates that $1 billion in additional exports can generate 42,700 jobs. Thus, the export potential we identify could mean somewhere between 300,000 and 500,000 additional jobs for Canadians.
I should like to stress that this is the first point that we hope to make today. It is not just a question of statistics; it is Canadian jobs that we are talking about. If we can do a better job of exporting to world markets, then the employment situation in this country is bound to improve. Before we can do that, we have to accept some of the harsh realities, however. For example, we have allowed ourselves, largely through the efforts of this Government, to drift into a position where today we are taxed on average, 20 per cent higher in Canada than are our cousins in the United States. That is a load that Canadians must carry, be they in business or the employees of those businesses, that our cousins do not have to cover when they are getting ready to compete with us in world markets.
Compared to our main trading partner, the United States, we have a deficit on a per capita basis which is twice the size of theirs. Oddly enough, in the United States the government is worried about the deficit, while in Canada we have a Government that tries to rationalize the deficit that is a burden on every Canadian, not just on those living today, but on future generations as well.
Is it not odd, in this connection, that we have a Government so totally out of step that it sends the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) to the United States to sell, as he says, "not goods, but goodwill"? It is not goodwill that we should primarily be trying to export to the United States, Mr. Speaker, but goods. If we can sell the Americans more Canadian-made goods, presumably the goodwill is there, else they would not buy.
November 15, 1982

While the Minister of State for International Trade is in the United States selling, not goods but goodwill, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is in France seeing the only remaining socialist government that he can make friends with, among major countries, on the basis that he wants to have an alternative deal to counteract the United States market in North America. Talk about spitting and sucking at the same time, Mr. Speaker. One Minister goes to the United States saying "let's have goodwill, let's do more business with you," while the Prime Minister goes to socialist France to try to curry favour with his only remaining friend among the Big Seven, the only socialist government he can find to talk to.
Let me go back, Mr. Speaker. Having this high deficit, this high taxation phenomenon in Canada, is it any wonder that we now find that we have the highest unemployment level of any of the major industrial nations and almost double the level of inflation that they are currently experiencing in the United States or in the United Kingdom? The short answer is that the 15-year program that this NDP-Liberal Government alliance has thrust on the Canadian economy has not worked.
The golden rule which we in the House can accept when we are looking for a new direction is that the socialist model has not worked and certainly will not work in the future. I say this because I believe we must come to grips with the real problem facing Canada today. We must allow the free enterprise system, the private sector, once again to get on with the job of creating wealth in the country and leave it to government to decide how, if necessary, it wants to redistribute that wealth. Also we must ensure that government, instead of intervening more, will intervene less as far as the economy is concerned.
I say this on three levels. First, if this Government wants to map out a new industrial strategy for Canada, it should deregulate rather than regulate further and generally have less control of the private sector than has been the experience over the past ten to 15 years. Second, it should consider less government spending, less give-aways and less bail-outs than has been its custom over that ten to 15 year period, encouraged as it has been by the socialists to our left. Finally, it must reharness the personal initiative and inventive spirit in Canada and give Canadians a chance to be free once again to participate in the prosperity upon which the country can build and grow, compared with the dull, dull performance of recent years. I say "dull performance" because we are absolutely last among major industrial countries in the area of productivity. As far as research and development are concerned, we are virtually at last spot. In short, we are not devoting ourselves to the rebuilding of Canada in the 1980s which we should be getting on with.
If I may, I should like to stress three points. I believe that Canada can rebuild in the 1980s. I believe it can regain some of the momentum which it lost if we promote exports in a more aggressive manner than we have been doing. Only this weekend I spoke with a chap who has extensive knowledge of world markets. He said that the word he hears wherever he goes in
Supply
the world is that Canada does not so much sell its goods abroad; the world buys our goods. In truth, we are not out there selling the way Canada could and should be selling.
The second point is that we must get on with capitalizing our industry. We must hit dead the bogey that somehow profits are wrong and that we must almost be ashamed to use the word. Another word for profits is jobs. To the degree that we can create the wherewithal through profits, we create the investment funds needed to build up productivity and job opportunities lacking in Canada at the present time.
We must process our resources to a much greater extent than we have been doing in recent years. Surely we must learn our lesson, as the Science Council of Canada pointed out so effectively in its November, 1981 booklet entitled "Hard Times-Hard Choices". Surely we have learned the lesson that we cannot expect employment in Canada if we systematically ship resources to some other country, allow them to manufacture the goods and only import manufactured goods. As was mentioned by the Science Council, we are the most open country in the world as far as such trade is concerned.
For those who have perhaps forgotten what the Science Council pointed out a year ago, let me read into the record what appears on page 15 of the booklet:
-Canada already stands unduly exposed. As recent studies have shown, few countries are as willing to allow ready access to their domestic markets as Canada is, and it is debatable whether we have gained significantly from this exposure. Canada already imports more duty free, finished manufactured goods-even excluding automotive goods-than do the U.S., Japan and the European Economic Community combined.
Surely that is a startling statement-a country of 24 million people importing more manufactured goods than those three large common markets combined, Japan, the European Common Market and the United States common market.
Let me continue. Accepting that we have to process our resources to a greater extent than we do at present, let me touch upon the entire area of research and development and its potential if we started diverting some of the money spent in the country and investing in the future. As far as our resources are concerned, let us think not only of what we have to dig out of the ground, mine or extract from an oil well. Let us think of our potential in water which has not perhaps been exploited to the present time. When we look at the lights above us, we should remember that that electricity was literally generated a few seconds ago; but because we have not learned how to store it, the electricity not instantly used is either never generated or lost for all time. Why cannot we set upon a research and development program whereby we will learn how to store water power we generate, hydroelectric power, so that it may be used, not instantly, as is our habit, but over a prolonged period? This is one of our challenges.
We hear in energy debates about oil and gas expenditures, Petro-Canada and whatnot. We should take a look at the glass of water sitting upon my desk and think about the energy which is in it, in the form of hydrogen and oxygen, which makes up water, H20. In short, some day a way to harness the hydrogen will be discovered, and we will have one of the

November 15, 1982
Supply
greatest forces the world has ever seen. Why cannot Canada be a pioneer in that type of inventive work? If we could hand some funds over to those who are almost begging for funding to allow them to get on with such research, we would not have to worry about energy shortages. A country which has 25 per cent of the fresh water supply in the world should never have to say to the rest of the world that it is short of energy. We would not have to do so if we set our minds to research and development which would unearth the secret and allow us to harness this potential.
Let me go into some other fields. At the present time research and development takes roughly $900 million of federal funds. That seems a huge amount of money until we start identifying where the Government spends other amounts of money. For example, we have in Supplementary Estimates before the House a request to spend $200 million for further capitalization of Canadair and a further $200 million capitalization for de Havilland. Those two amounts, making a total of $400 million, will be coupled to the $1.7 billion that we have already committed to help out those two firms. In short, that is $2 billion for two companies, and for those two companies alone it is twice the total Federal Government commitment to be made this year for research and development for the entire nation.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we could take a portion of those funds and use it for research and development, we would find a much greater reward down the road than by leaving that money to be invested in those two enterprises.
The United Way Appeal in Canada, much to its credit, has raised or hopes to raise $110 million this year. That is 55 per cent of the amount of capital that we are being asked to put into Canadair alone. For example, the Heart Foundation, the Cancer Fund, the Terry Fox Marathon of Hope, have each raised or hope to raise about $25 million this year. That amount, which is for research, is a small amount compared to what this Government dishes out for some of its favourite projects in the form of bail-outs for various corporations, both private and public.

Mr. Speaker, we should accept that it is no longer a question of identifying the problem or a question of saying what should we do in Canada, because the solutions are there. It is time for the Government to get on with the job. The Government should say that what it is going to do is create the atmosphere in this country that will allow our potential to be reharnessed once again. I suggest that it begin not by apologizing for the free enterprise system but by saying that the free enterprise system is the solution and not the problem. It is the Government that is the problem.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Would the Hon. Member entertain a question?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, for the past 30 minutes I have listened intently to the Hon. Member's speech. I was waiting and waiting for him to give this House and the nation the Conservative Party's definitive industrial strategy. The Hon. Member has not given one example. Could he very briefly give us a few specifics of the Conservative Party's industrial strategy that for two and a half years we, in this House and the nation, have been waiting for?
What about yours?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that we have the attention of the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn). As he probably knows, we have six other speakers to follow me. They will fill in exactly the industrial strategy that he is looking for. However, let me outline three things that he will hear if he is just a little patient.
First, we think there is room to insure, much as NHA mortgages are insured, business loans in this country. Second, we think there is room to introduce industrial revenue bonds for small businesses in this country, similar to what one finds in many of the states in the United States of America, but greatly needed in Canada if we want to get small businesses reharnessed and people back to work. Again, we are going to suggest that it is time that the precedent, if you like, set by the Ontario Government be endorsed by the Federal Government. The Ontario Government in its Small Business Development Act has a program which raises money for small businesses. It facilitates the raising of that money by making grants available up to 30 per cent. This program should be endorsed by the federal Government and added to, instead of frustrated by the federal Government, something which has been going on in this country.
We have many other points like that, Mr. Speaker, but I do not want to take away the making of those points from my colleagues who will be speaking during the course of this debate.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today gives us the opportunity to speak to a very important issue that is facing the country, namely the need for an industrial or an economic development strategy that I believe has been sadly lacking for the past 30 years or 40 years.
I suppose we could have an agreement in this House that the most important priority and the most important question to solve is that of providing jobs for about 1.5 million Canadians who do not have jobs today. That is the most important priority. There is nothing that is as difficult for a person or for a family than to be faced with unemployment, to be able to work but not have a job because of the state of Canada's economy. If we look to other countries in the world we find that the unemployment statistics in Canada are among the
November 15, 1982

worst, if not the worst, of the industrialized states. We also find that the long-term situation looks very bad from all the reports that we see.
In this country we have an economy that is disintegrating before our very eyes. Why is that happening? What is the difference between Canada and the United States, Canada and Japan, or Canada and Europe? Why do we have unemployment problems that are much higher here than in other countries? Why does the long-term look so much worse in Canada than in other countries?
I think there is an answer to that question. There is a major difference between us and other countries. Other countries decided a long time ago that they would control, own and direct their own economies. We in Canada do not do that. We have more foreign ownership, foreign control and foreign investment in the equity stance than any other industrialized country in the world. As a result of that, we are now reaping the benefits of a very truncated branch-line economy where we export capital and import unemployment from other countries around the world.
I think the time has come for this country to have a new vision of what we are about and where we are going. As I listened to members of the Conservative Party today, and as I have listened to them over the last few months when they talk about the whole question of foreign investment and economic direction in this country, I think they have picked up the mantle of the late C. D. Howe. They have picked up his mantle of unfettered continentalism. I wonder what John Diefenbaker or Sir John A. Macdonald would think of this Party to my right today if they heard the talk about removing FIRA, getting rid of all the inhibitions of foreign investment and, in effect, becoming the fifty-first state of the United States of America?
That is nonsense.
That Party has played the tune of Ronald Reagan in this country. It has taken FIRA and what really is a mouse and created a monster out of it.
You are wrong.

At one time that Party, under the leadership of people like Sir John A. Macdonald up to John Diefenbaker, did have a bit of respect for Canadian economic nationalism and for creating a Canada owned by Canadians. But we see the same thing across the way. I am glad to hear a Liberal interjecting at this point. In my opinion, what we are seeing is a massive retreat concerning FIRA, a massive retreat in trying to own Canada.
I remember the 1980 election campaign very well. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was the Leader of the Opposition at that time. He travelled across this country promising that if he were re-elected, he would not only maintain FIRA but would strengthen it and make it into an agency with teeth on behalf of Canadians. He said in Toronto on February 13 that, if elected, the Liberal Party would "make sure that FIRA's mandate will be broadened to include the periodic
Supply
review of all foreign firms of large size to assess the performance of these companies in such areas as export promotion and research and development". He also said in the Throne Speech a few months later, in April:
The new government wants to expand the opportunities for independent Canadian-owned enterprise, especially in highgrowth areas like advanced technology.
The government's commitment is to ensuring that foreigh-owned companies operate in accordance with Canadian industrial goals.
He also said in the Throne Speech:
-the Foreign Investment Review Act will be amended to provide for performance reviews of how large foreign firms are meeting the test of bringing substantial benefits to Canada. As well, amendments will be introduced to ensure that major acquisition proposals by foreign companies will be publicized prior to a government decision on their acceptability. The Government will assist Canadian companies wishing to repatriate assets or to bid for ownership or control of companies subject to takeover offers by non-Canadians.
What do we see some two months later? We see a tremendous retreat by the Liberal Government opposite. Not only does it not try to strengthen FIRA; it wants to make it weaker in response to pressure from the administration of President Reagan in the United States. I suggest that this Government is once again opening up our doors to unregulated and uncontrolled foreign investment that is stealing jobs from Canadians, moving billions of Canadian dollars to the United States, Japan or western Europe in the form of profits or dividends to foreign investors.
This is what Governments in this country have done in the past. In fact, in 1981 our deficit in the balance of payments was $9.1 billion. That money could have been used to create jobs for Canadians, to develop an economic strategy which would strengthen the nation and make it more productive and cost competitive internationally. Instead, our banks are lending money to foreign investors who are investing in Canada, creating unemployment in Canada while creating employment in other countries of the world.
One only needs to review the statistics. According to Statistics Canada, the branch plants of foreign-owned firms import nearly five times as many foreign goods in the manufacturing sector as Canadian firms. Much of this is done from the branch plant to the parent in the United States or elsewhere in the world. Many of these goods are imported despite the fact that it has no real bearing in terms of a company's efficiency or competitiveness.
There is very little research and development conducted in this country. Research and development is not carried out in this country because so much of our economy is foreign owned. To illustrate this, I have figures that show that in 1973 only 2.7 per cent of Canadian manufacturing firms had R and D facilities operating in this country. If you look at the figures for research and development for 1975, Canada is probably at the bottom of the list of developed countries, certainly at the bottom of the list of all the OECD nations. Research and development expenditure should be doubled in this country.

November 15, 1982
*
Supply
One reason for the lack of research and development is that many of our firms in key industries are foreign owned and involve very little product innovation. In the United States, for example, 1.84 per cent of sales in all industries went back into R and D. In Canada, only 0.78 per cent, less than half, went into research and development. Domestically, Canadian firms put up 0.86 per cent of their sales for research and development while foreign controlled firms in this country only put up 0.71 per cent of their sales. This proves once again that foreign controlled firms are less likely to put money into research and development, the creation of jobs in Canada and the creation of products that are more cost efficient, which would create world trade and provide Canadians with more jobs.
In addition, we find that approximately 58 per cent of our exports are in the resource sector, which provides little in terms of employment because they are capital-intensive industries. On the import side, however, we find that 60 per cent of our imports are in the area of highly finished goods and products. I maintain that as long as we do not control our economy as Canadians we will not be involved in the processing and development that should be done in this country.
In 1970 we had a manufacturing deficit of some $2.5 billion. That had escalated to some $17.8 billion by 1980. By 1981 it was around $21 billion. In the automobile sector-despite the auto pact with the United States-we see an accumulating deficit that is skyrocketing. The deficit in 1980 was approximately $10 billion. It is probably reaching closer to $15 billion in 1982 despite the fact that we have an agreement with the United States which is supposed to give Canadians a fair share of production jobs in accordance with the sale of cars in this country. In 1976, for example, our share of car purchases was 8.9 per cent and our share of production was only 7 per cent. Despite the agreement, we are getting short changed and, as a result, we are exporting jobs to the United States of America.
This same situation is true for almost any industry one wishes to consider. We can consider machinery, which is labour-intensive and innovative. It is important in terms of new technology. Our trade imbalance in machinery for 1980 was $6.9 billion. If Canadians were to overcome this tremendous deficit in our balance of trade in machinery, we could create some 69,000 production jobs alone in Canada.
Let us consider machinery with respect to each sector. Canada is a major agricultural producer. However, we have a deficit in agricultural equipment of $1.3 billion. We have a deficit of $1 billion in the mining and construction industries despite our resources. We have a deficit of $563 million in powered generation equipment for the year 1980. The deficit with respect to industrial machinery is $898 million. We have a $1 billion deficit in rolling equipment and machine tools. Many of these deficits involve sectors in which we should be specializing and leading the world. We should have surpluses in our products such as agriculture, mines and hydro. These resources are in abundance in Canada. If the Europeans, Japanese or Americans had this abundance of resources they would be producing in abundance, exporting around the world and creating thousands of jobs, many of which would be highly paid and highly skilled. However, because of lack of imagination and the chicken mentality of governments over the years,
we do not have the nerve to control our own economy as the Americans, the Europeans and the Japanese have always done.
In the area of high technology we already have a deficit in computer and office products in 1981 of some $1.77 billion. At that rate, some 60,000 jobs will be lost between now and 1985. Yet we have a Government that is just now beginning to think of developing a strategy in Canada for advanced technology. That type of approach is just not acceptable.
Despite those statistics which show the massive deficits in the balance of payments, the export of jobs and the lack of control over our economy, I am amazed that the Government is now retreating on such a small agency as FIRA. The Conservative Party has turned aside its traditions and is now almost unpatriotic in terms of what is once stood for and what it is now calling for-more unfettered foreign investment and the dismantling or the pulling of the teeth of the Foreign Investment Review Act.
It is beyond me why we as Canadians do not have more imagination or fortitude than we have seen in the past. I have an interesting quote about how Canadians lose jobs from a United States Senate Committee hearing on July 8, 1981. Mr. Harvey Bale is assistant trade representative for investment policy in the U.S. I think we should very carefully listen to his words. He said:
We believe that U.S. foreign direct investment has also made a contribution to employment in the United States through the link between exports and investment. Much of our trade with foreign countries originates with orders placed by the subsidiaries of U.S. companies located overseas. For example 75 per cent of our exports to the 300 largest companies in Canada originates from the subsidiaries of U.S. firms.
The purpose of much of the foreign investment in our country is to create jobs in other countries around the world. I maintain that the time has come when we as Canadians should do as other developed countries have done, namely, take control of our economy and ensure that key sectors are developed and owned by Canadians through an application of public ownership, social ownership, private ownership, cooperative ownership and the like.
Petro-Canada controls or dominates only 12 per cent or 14 per cent of the market, but is only the fifth largest company. We should ensure that Petro-Canada becomes the largest company in the country and controls over 50 per cent of the market. These are examples of what we will have to do. We must also ensure that foreign companies operating in Canada, in proportion to their sales, will ensure the same proportion of research and development, expansion of their plants and creation of jobs. Many countries in the world have those kinds of rules and regulations. France, Germany and Japan were virtually destroyed during the Second World War. Those countries decided that they would rebuild their economies by ensuring that their nationals, their people, were in control so that they could make decisions and provide employment. Today, all three of those countries are doing better than our country.


November 15, 1982

Since 1960 we have seen our standard of living, which was formerly second in the world, plummet to tenth place or even worse, depending upon how one reads the statistics, in terms of standard of living, or average income, around the world.
Therefore, it has become imperative that we have a national industrial strategy which will deal with certain key sectors which we should be developing, sectors which are of natural advantage to us, such as agricultural products and other resources. We must specialize in those areas and process those resources and food products much more than we do now before export. We must develop machinery, agricultural or mining, to provide our own market and to supply markets around the world. We must do things like that if we are to create jobs for Canadians.
Then we must consider other areas of natural benefit to Canada, such as transportation and communications. We are a big country and we must develop ways of moving quickly and communicating quickly and efficiently. We should specialize in trains and communications equipment. It should be ourselves, for example, rather than the French and the Japanese who have the fastest trains in the world. It should be ourselves who are exporting technology to other parts of the world, rather than the French and the Japanese. The same is true in the communications sector where we do have some technology, some Canadian know-how which is very good. We are a world leader in that sector and we should develop other sectors more quickly.
I would very briefly like to refer to the area of advanced technology. We have heard many reports which state that we are lagging behind. We have an industry which is being run down, an industrial sector which is disintegrating very rapidly. Unless we make some changes very quickly we will be in even more serious trouble in the years that lie ahead.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you are about to stand, and if I may have two or three more minutes, I will wind up my remarks.

speechtext: Is there unanimous agreement that the time allotted to the Hon. Member may be extended?
Agreed.

1 wanted to wind up my remarks by making an appeal to the House to consider what is happening to our various sectors, industrial, steel, footwear, textiles, and to many industries which have provided jobs in the past. In almost all cases we find that technology is moving very rapidly, but unless we change and innovate we will lose even more jobs in these sectors. In the future it will be very important to innovate here in Canada, to ensure that development of hardware, computers, new gadgets and technology occurs right here in this country. It will also be equally important to ensure that we control the technological revolution. We as Canadian people must introduce it in a planned and sensible way as a result of consultation with ordinary working people, the Provinces, the farmers, women and people who will be most affected by micro-chip technology, new hardware or new software.
Supply
It is very important that we start training our young people for the new society which is already with us. It is startling to me to find that there are 40 times more people in electrical engineering schools in Japan than in this country. The Japanese are preparing for the society which is already with us. Twice as many people graduate from their schools than in the United States, even though they have half the population of the United States. We are moving into an era of robotics and fully automated factories, yet we are not producing and planning for the future which is lying ahead.
As my last comment in this particular debate, I suggest it would be constructive if all three Parties in the House were to establish a special committee on the social and economic impact of advanced technology which would provide some input from elected parliamentarians as to how we want the country to evolve and develop in the next 20 or 30 years. If we do not do it, it will arrive from other places. Technology will be imported from Japan, western Europe and the United States. Once again, it will not be Canadian owned and controlled and perhaps will not even be developed in this country as much as in the past. Because of growing perfectionism in the world, we will be importing much more than we imported in the past. So I think it is important in this Parliament that we form a special committee to study the impact, socially and economically, of the new technology. That would be a part, I would hope, of a new industrial and economic strategy that we need very badly. Its priority must be, as I said, to ensure that industrial and economic activity in this country is owned, controlled and developed by Canadians for Canadians.
We have the resources and we have the people. All we need is the dream, the goal, the vision; and I am sure that, with the goodwill of the Canadian people, we could create a country that is second to none in the twenty-first century.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to be participating in the debate this afternoon on a motion by the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), and I would ask the Members opposite to be patient as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) will be rising in the House later today.
I listened very carefully to the comments made by the Member for York-Peel just now, when he talked about promoting our goods and increasing exports, but I did not hear him making any suggestions on how our exports should be increased.

The Hon. Member talked about frustration. Well, there is frustration in Canada, everyone knows that, and 1.3 million are unemployed. There are different areas of frustration. He says Canadians know we can do better. We all know that. We had a lesson on inventions in the nineteenth century. We had a talk about pioneers. We even had a lesson in history and one in

November 15, 1982
Supply
chemistry, but not one word about how to increase productivity or exportation.
The Hon. Member for York-Peel talked about regularization. I think he felt like talking about privatization, but the fact is that whenever he starts talking about that, Petro-Canada comes into his speeches, and that is kaput as far as the Tory party is concerned. Tories are not supposed to talk about Petro-Canada.
[ Translation]
If 1 take the last part of the Hon. Member's motion, Mr. Speaker, it says, and I quote:
-and to provide incentives for training opportunities and to the private sector for new, and increased levels of research and development in Canada.
1 wonder where the Hon. Member was on October 28 of this year when we had first reading of Bill C-136, a bill that is concerned with small businesses and will help small businesses contracting loans between June 28, 1982 and March 31, 1983, to finance acquisition of new depreciable assets or to finance research and development. That he did not mention. Did he mention the day, Monday, November 8, when the bill was passed on second reading and referred to committee? No, he did not. Are the Progressive Conservatives afraid to mention certain measures this government has brought before Parliament? Mr. Speaker, I think they are more interested in talking about bringing down this government and about their leadership than in providing constructive criticism aimed at helping Canadians to break through the present economic impasse.
Mr. Speaker, it was indeed very appropriate that Bill C-136 should be introduced on October 28, during the third annual small business week. This event is sponsored by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Federal Development Bank for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the general public and business people in particular the various ways in which the federal, provincial and municipal governments can help with their administrative operations. We had exhibits with information booths across Canada.
At the end of a full week here in the Outaouais region, prizes were awarded to various individuals for outstanding accomplishment in business during the past year. When the prizes were being awarded, the Outaouais was visited by one of the ministers in the Quebec government, who was eager to satisfy the separatists and decided to shoot off a few arrows from the other side of the river. He was in Hull at the University du Quebec, and I would like to make it clear to Minister Biron that the whole week dedicated to small business was apolitical and had been organized by the Outaouais Development Corporation, the Federal Development Bank, and business people. Instead of making political remarks that certainly did nothing to enhance the well-being of the people or small businesses, if the minister had told people: Listen, we are going to help you, we are going to reduce income taxes since you are paying the highest taxes in Canada, we are going to
reduce income taxes so that you can live as well as your counterparts in Ontario and the United States. That would have helped business people. Or he might have told people involved in the transport business: Listen, we are going to reduce the tax on gas so that you will be able to compete with other people instead of paying $5, $6, $7 and sometimes $10 more to fill the tank in your car or bus.
Were these people going to get a refund from the provincial government? No, Mr. Speaker, the minister did not mention that. He criticized the federal government as if the latter were still largely responsible for the slump Quebec is experiencing at the present time. I know there are separatists who are going to say that if Quebec had its own resources, in other words, if Quebec alone had the authority to levy taxes, it might be possible. I simply cannot believe that some separatists are still using this argument, namely, that if they had control over all their resources, in other words, if they were independent, they could afford more or less the same standard of living and the same taxation levels as other provinces.
In an article that appeared in Le Droit on April 16, and 1 am going back that far because it is important and we tend to forget, it was said, and I quote:
Ottawa is giving more than it is taking away from Quebec.
In 1980, the federal government spent $14.9 billion in Quebec and collected only $10.5 billion in revenue and taxes-
That is what independence will mean: more taxes. Our people pay the highest taxes in Canada, and if we have to pay four billion dollars more, where are we going to raise it? I feel this has to be said, Mr. Speaker, because certain leaders and certain ministers in the provincial government are making bold accusations without being able to substantiate them, in order to confuse people and perhaps smooth the way for some of our separatist friends.
To get back to Bill C-136, Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that this legislation would help businesses finance acquisition of new depreciable assets or finance research and development, between June 29, 1982 and March 31, 1983, by making them eligible for an interest subsidy, provided by the Canadian government, of up to 4 per cent of the amount borrowed from the bank. The federal government will pay directly into the account of the borrower a sum representing up to 4 per cent of the amount borrowed. It is understood that as soon as the interest rate is down to 12 per cent, the subsidy is reduced accordingly. That is a concrete example of what this government has done to promote small business research and development.
The Hon. Member talked about increasing exports of Canadian manufactured goods. He does not seem to be familiar with the 6 and 5 program. The program is not an end in itself but provides the means, that is, by reducing salaries, Canadians will be able to bring down the rate of inflation and consequently interest rates, and thus increase investment and
November 15, 1982

the number of jobs available, so that in the final analysis, we will be reducing the unemployment rate. In fact, increasing productivity was the purpose of the 6 and 5 program, and this is extremely important in the present economic situation, if we are to become at all competitive and compete with other countries who are producing the same goods we are.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should discuss some of the measures this government has taken since 1980 with respect to industry. This governemnt has made an effort to create a climate that is favourable to investment, whatever the members opposite care to think. The government has taken measures aimed at ensuring that funds will be available for viable projects and provided loan guarantees for both small and certain larger companies. I will have more to say about that later on. I take the liberty of speaking in such a way that my friends opposite will remember. We are not all mean Liberals, we are not all mean Government members. There are certain things which ought to be appreciated. Michelin tires, for instance. The Canadian Government will award $42 million in grants to promote a program which will eventually trigger a $400 million-plus investment by Michelin. Mr. Speaker, I believe that will be in the Atlantic Provinces-I cannot recall which one, but in any event it does show that the federal government has taken the initiative in that field. Some people raised hell and said all kinds of things about the Chrysler deal, but the fact remains that it was not an outright grant but a loan guarantee. Unfortunately, they are now talking about going on strike. That made it possible for the workers to keep their jobs and there is the possibility of a $150 million loan guarantee. Massey-Ferguson and their $126 million loan guarantee was a similar case and again the purpose was to keep people working.
We now have a program which has been implemented to modernize the textile industry so that it will be competitive with other countries marketing similar products. Modernization is the order of the day in the forest industry as well because one out of ten workers depends on it for a living, which makes it a key sector in Canada. Gatineau's CIP in my riding was awarded $6 million by the central government under a federal-provincial agreement and the MacLaren Company was also granted $6 or $7 million to update its facilities. Mr. Speaker, millions of dollars have been spent for a newsprint industry in Amos. 1 do not know how many millions were spent by the companies which own the plants, but still the federal government has done its share to launch that industry.
This government has also approved the five-year program of the National Research Council of Canada. Mention was made
Adjournment Motion
of research earlier. An amount of $48 million has been allocated to promote research and development, provide information to small businesses and encourage the private sector to use advanced technology. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but I see that my time is going quickly. But it must be kept in mind that it is the private sector which will get us out of this difficult situation. We shall be called all sorts of names, such as socialists and the right or left arm of the New Democratic Party, and so on, but that does not bother me. More important, it still remains that the Liberal Party now believes that the private sector will get us out of this fix. The federal government wants to play an active part in support of the private sector and help small and medium-size businesses and the private sector as a whole to become self-sufficient.
We have taken some measures and we shall continue to do so, but we are willing to act in a spirit of consultation, cooperation and harmony. And when I say harmony, Mr. Speaker, I think you know what I mean. There is nothing you cannot do with the people behind you and when all three levels of government and everyone else put up a common front. Then, you can do anything. Someone said earlier that the Canadian people know they can do better, but in this spirit of harmony, co-operation and collaboration, the results can only be positive.
Mutual trust is essential, Mr. Speaker, to economic recovery. No federal or provincial policy or program and no management or labour initiative can get Canada out of the recession unless everyone works together, and this includes the members of the Conservative Party and the NDP. It is only with their co-operation that we can succeed.
