The record of the Liberal Government during the 1970s and even during the 1960s in the area of research and development is appalling. 1 think much is already contained in various commissions and studies, to which the Hon. Member referred, regarding the low level of research and development in Canada during the seventies. The percentage of R and D as a percentage of the gross national product dropped to 0.9 per cent. That was around the same level as the expenditure of research and development in countries such as Ireland and Portugal. What happened during the seventies, the years, the decade of Liberal neglect, was that our university research facilities have deteriorated. Studies have shown the deplorable condition of the equipment in our universities. There is no immediate prospect of funding to modernize the equipment which is so badly needed by the research community in Canada. Indeed, if the Government were really committeed to having a strong research and development sector in Canada, I would suggest it would immediately introduce emergency funding to update the existing equipment in our universities. It would be a significant and also a symbolic gesture to show the Government's commitment to improved R and D in this country.
During the seventies also, under the leadership of the Liberals in Government, we saw a massive brain drain. In fact, the projections are that even if we do accomplish our 1.5 per cent of GNP toward R and D, the goal which was read to us during the Speech from the Throne which opened this Parliament, there is grave doubt that there will be enough trained manpower to fill all the scientific positions because of the starving of funds for the scientific community.
Much has been done to blame workers in this country. It is a favourite pastime of our Conservative friends and the Liberal Government to blame Canadian labour. They say Canadian labour is not productive. I would suggest that the fault lies in part with the Government opposite, because during the 1970s, when industry should have been reinvesting in research and development and in more modern plants and equipment, it did not do so. There was a dismally low level of research and development in Canada, below 0.9 per cent of the GNP. In part, both Government and private industry are to blame. The fact that major industries in this country are branch plants of larger multinationals has meant that very little research and development has occurred in the Canadian subsiduaries. It has meant that very little capital has been reinvested in new equipment. In other words, the cream was taken off. Dividends were distributed to shareholders all over the world without the desirable amounts of money being returned for new equipment. Both industry and Government, and industry's lackeys, the Conservatives, have the gall to put the blame on Canadian workers.
To me, productivity is very simple. It is the difference between a person who saws 24 hours a day with a handsaw and another who spends three hours sawing with an electric saw. The person with the electric saw, of course, will be more productive than the person with the handsaw, and it does not matter how motivated they are in their work. The person with
the handsaw can have the highest motivation and put in 24 hours a day, yet he will produce less than the person with the electric saw, with some new equipment, with the means to produce more.
Yes, indeed, there is a need for an industrial strategy and, in fact, I would say there is also a need for a social industrial strategy.
The underfunding of the social sciences was another area of Liberal neglect during the seventies. It consisted of the starving of funds for social sciences in this country and the squeeze on the universities. Surely the Government opposite must share a fair amount of the blame for that. We in the New Democratic Party have been calling for an industrial and social strategy for years. In fact, it is a major tenet of our philosophy that one must have some national strategies and establish some national goals in order to bring together industry, science and government into a cohesive whole. If one does not have these strategies, and if one relies upon the blind mechanism of the "market", one will essentially have economic and social anarchy and, indeed, that is occurring today.
I therefore find it somewhat amusing that the Conservatives, in their Opposition motion, should be calling for an industrial strategy, yet most of the speeches I have heard today suggest that that strategy should be one of letting the marketplace take care of things. They suggest that we should just let Government back off, and let the captains of industry, banking, finance, et cetera, make those decisions which will drive the engine of industry and create new science, new research and new developments. I find it just amazing that, on the one hand, they are calling for an industrial strategy and yet, on the other hand, they are saying that the public has no influence or important part to play in the economic life of this country or in the degree of research and development we will have in the future. I find it amazing, especially when I hear people in the Conservative Party who should know better mouthing that line. In this age of rapid scientific discovery and innovation, the public sector has a tremendous need. In the areas of protecting public health and the environment, there is a tremendous need for Government regulation, and concern. However, my Conservative friends say we should do away with all these regulations.
No, we do not.

Yet they are the first ones to complain when private industry has failed to live up to its public responsibilities or when the Government has failed to enforce the public interest. May I take as an example, the case of urea formaldehyde, a new technological innovation which has been proven dangerous to human health. Are the Conservatives suggesting that we should have even less public regulation and have more urea formaldehyde type of situations occurring?
Who led business into it?

Is this the case? However, when the accident occurs, they insist that Government should solve the problem and fix up the mess.

A conscious public effort is needed to withstand that pull south. The same is true in the area of research and development. While the Conservatives call for more research and development, and I totally agree with them, how do they propose to get more research and development?
Every major study has indicated that the main problem with research and development in this country is that the private sector in Canada does not invest in R and D as they do in the United States, Japan, Germany, and Great Britain.

Because every study on the subject has indicated that the branch plant economy, the nature of our economy, dictates against the development of our industry in this country. That is the result of studies of economists, sociologists and accountants. These are not ideological figures; they are not

political figures; this is the bare-bones reality of where we are at in this country.
Where are the solutions and how are we going to come to these solutions? Unfortunately, the solutions are not alluded to in the motion and the speeches we have heard today.
There is a tremendous need for an industrial-social strategy. Many countries in the Western world are experiencing unemployment at significant levels. There is no immediate hope that that situation will change in the next couple of years. It seems that the economies of the Western world have reached a certain plateau. Many governments now are making a mad dash, hoping to gain some leadership in the only growth area in most economies, the high-tech industries.
The interesting contradiction is that most of those technologies will cause increased unemployment. The new microtechnologies will mean the massive lay-off of hundreds of thousands of clerks. What is missing is a national, social and economic strategy because we are going into the twenty-first century, whether we like it or not. We have essentially two choices. One is to proceed in an unplanned way, in a reactive way, trying to solve the problems as they are created. The alternative is to plan for the changes; to develope some strategies in order to control the pace and direction of these changes so they will have a minimum negative effect on Canadians. Those are the two choices we have.
To me a national economic and social strategy will bring together members of industry, labour, universities and the scientific community. There should be a give-and-take and some co-operation. The only way we are going to survive as a society is through that co-operation because these new technologies will be coming and they will have both a positive and a negative impact upon our society. Yet what I see from the Liberals is just continuing blunder after blunder after blunder. We are going to blunder into the twenty-first century.
They are following your policies.

My Hon. friend from the Conservative Party says that they are following our policies. May I suggest that what the Liberals have done is to give Government a bad name. Years of mismanagement have brought disrespect to the public sector, and 1 blame the Liberals for that. The Liberals like the Conservatives, they have never believed in a strong public role in managing the economy. That is why it is an ongoing program of blunder and blunder.
We are going to go into the twenty-first century and we are going to have technological innovation, whether it comes from within Canada or without, or whether other countries are going to take the lead. In fact, many other countries now are investing huge sums of money into R and D. I refer to France where agreements between labour, industry and government have meant a massive increase in their R and D expenditure. They are going to take a massive leap, especially in the fields of microtechnology and bio-engineering. Telidon, or their

There are certain questions I believe we should ask in discussing R and D. We should also be concerned about the qualitative and not the quantitative aspect of R and D. Research and development for whom? Who will benefit? Who will pay what price? Perhaps we should also look at other forms of technologies. There is a whole other field rarely discussed called appropriate technology. These are the technologies like the innovation of new airtight wood stoves that allow massive decreases in fuel consumption, that reduce the cost of living of average Canadians, make us as a society more self-sufficient and less dependent upon non-renewable resources like the fossil fuels.
Perhaps there are other innovations that will reduce the cost of living that Canadians have to face every year. Those would be technologies and innovations that would reduce the cost of living, that would make it easier for Canadian men and women to live and would require less income on their part.
There are new technologies in alternate energy. Perhaps we can develop new technologies in home construction. I estimate that the Canadian family has to spend up to $750,000 in their lifetime to pay for their housing. Perhaps we can develop new forms, new technologies and new means by which housing can be supplied so that it is no longer necessary for an average family to earn $750,000 just to pay for their housing, therefore, making it less necessary to earn that income.
Perhaps we will never again have full employment. If that is the case, how can those who are unemployed, through no fault of their own, gain the income to buy life's necessities, how can they survive? Are they, as victims, to be blamed, to be called lazy and parasites on society? I do not think so.
I think there are possibilities for Canadian ingenuity to develop other social forms, to develop appropriate technologies that would allow a meaningful existence to all people. We have the brain power, we have the resources. I know there is a natural will in the country to come together and work toward some collective goals. What we need is some leadership. We have not seen that leadership.
In conclusion I thank the movers of the motion for presenting this resolution. It is an important motion. I think it should be debated in terms of its full meaning. Perhaps out of such debates we can begin to come to some understanding as to what an industrial and social strategy really should include, if we are to survive as a society.

Member to make statements like that in this House, and I suggest to him that he should not make statements like that unless he is prepared to back them up with facts.

And less Grits.

Well, I guess that is one of the luxuries you have when you are in opposition. You can have your cake and eat it, too. We heard, again from the Hon. taxpayers of Canada for the development of our area. We have the problem of Chatham, and it is a very serious problem indeed. 1 reiterate, not one job has yet been lost.
Yet.

That is not a very small undertaking, Mr. Speaker. I suppose if you were losing that many jobs in Toronto there would be all kinds of Tory Members up on their hind legs yelling and screaming that the Government had to provide incentives to retain those jobs. Once the jobs were retained, of course, they would then be up on their feet yelling and screaming that the Government should not be involved. Just like the Hon. Member for Fundy Royal who never had any interest in the Miramichi until the announcement was made with regard to the stand-down of 416 Squadron at Chatham, and then all of a sudden his heart started to bleed. Well, that has not impressed a lot of people in the Miramichi, and I doubt that it will.
Neither have you.

Instead of
crocodile tears, our interest is in action. But we must solve problems like that, and I say, Mr. Speaker, that private industry alone will not solve them because private industry, if left to itself, will do exactly what the Tory Members over there want it to do; it will locate in the Edmontons, the Torontos, the Montreals, the Calgarys, the Windsors and Halifaxes, but it will not locate in the small rural areas of this country without incentive from Government, without grants to assist in the development. If anyone here can convince me, for instance, that Mitel would have gone to Buctouche without Government incentives, I am prepared to listen. But I say it would never have happened, and we will never have that type of industry or development on the Miramichi of New Brunswick without Government incentives and grants, and without persuading business to put their industries where the labour is. The Tories, of course, would have us move those workers to their part of the country, to the metropolitan areas of the country, rather than to provide the jobs and opportunities where the people

are, where they have grown up, and where they want their families to live and grow up.
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments about this motion which is quite relevant in the present economic context. I shall try to do so quickly since other Members also want to speak. I wish to congratulate the mover of this motion which, and I quote:
-condemns the Government for its failure to introduce its promised comprehensive industrial strategy-
-for which we have been waiting I do not know how many years. Mr. Speaker, I shall not go over some remarks about partisanship that I was somewhat shocked to hear in such an important debate. I listened closely to the criticisms which the last spokesman for the New Democratic Party levelled at the Progressive Conservative Party, but I think that the Canadian people realize that it was his own party that made it possible for this Government to return to power. It is not the first time that the New Democrats have sold out to the Liberal Party. I am thinking about 1974 and the following years. If one party should be held responsible for the loss of 400,000 to 500,000 jobs in Canada jointly with this Government that refused to maintain our tax credit on mortgage interests, which would have really given a new impetus to the building industry, it is certainly the New Democratic Party. It should be held as fully responsible as the present Government. There are limits! I shall not say too much about the NDP because we in Quebec are not very familiar with it, not even with the meaning of those three letters. I remember the candidate who opposed me in my constituency and the billboards that said: "NDP means No Drawing Power." This party is therefore not our main concern in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to go quickly over the comments made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley), who referred to the efforts made by this Government since 1981. It is obvious that the Government is making some effort; it is also obvious that it has acted as a fireman must act when a fire breaks out. Today's motion condemns the Government, and I think everyone will agree that it was not the Progressive Conservative Party that has wasted the time of this House during the last 20 years, considering the length of time it stayed in power. We are all well aware that in the last 20 years, except for a very brief period, we have had a Liberal administration which is responsible for our present problems.
Is there any need to refer to the thousands of bankruptcies, to unemployment which has increased tenfold in the last ten years or to the present situation? The Liberal Member who spoke before me stated that the private sector could not manage its own affairs effectively without the co-operation of
Supply
the Government. Mr. Speaker, we are well aware that within the framework of an industrial strategy, the Government will obviously have to develop an attractive climate for investment, that it must provide medium and long-term directions to private industry if it is willing to make room for private business, and that it must also provide additional assistance to certain disadvantaged sectors or regions. There is no doubt about that, but it must be within the framework of an industrial strategy and a medium and long-term economic policy. As concerns this economic policy and industrial strategy, Mr. Speaker, I shall not be able to devise solutions this evening, but common sense requires that I point out to the House that the government has not made every effort possible to develop such a strategy, which would mean, first of all, bringing together industry, namely investors, businessmen as well as unions- and if productivity is our goal, this is important-and, of course, the Government itself and the Departments concerned. To my knowledge, a real industrial strategy has not been brought before this House in the last 15 or 20 years. In my opinion, we have had no real industrial strategy. Of course, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has a clearly socialist view of the economy as a whole.
Anyway, our liberal friends know where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came from before leading the Liberal party. This is of significance, and I am serious about this, Mr. Speaker, because the NDP often complains about liberal policy. Well, the Prime Minister has a socialist approach and the liberals do not realize where the Prime Minister has led them. He has done such a bad job of implementing his socialist policy that the socialists will no longer support him, they can not vote in support. This is astounding. And it is a fact that the whole government approach is now distorted by the Prime Ministers' views. Well, the Liberal party was not leaning that way not so long ago, before the last fifteen years. I would simply ask honorable members to ponder seriously and honestly over the prevailing situation. There is no doubt that the outlook is bleak. Canadians are worried.
Canadian youth is losing hope, and why, Mr. Speaker? Because there has not been a genuine industrial strategy. What would have happened? The minister referred earlier to the aid extended for instance to Canadair and de Havilland. Is that creating one single new job right now? Not at all. This is another government effort to salvage what may be left. If we had had a genuine industrial policy or strategy, would the shoe or textile industries have gone through the hardships they have over these last few years? Of course, they will argue they have spent millions. The minister said so earlier. In the textile industry, there was a recommendation to grant millions of dollars, but to what end? To promote early retirement at age 50. Clearly, they have given up hope in the future of the textile industry. They are going to help other industries. How long did we have to wait for the minister to reinstate quotas in the

November 15, 1982
Supply
footwear industry? Five or six months, and in this House, Hon. Members opposite would invite me to put questions, because it was getting embarrassing for them to challenge the minister. Finally, the minister caught on, and I do not blame him too much for his efforts. He has been talking about it since 1981, but we know that an industrial strategy should have been established 20 years ago, and I feel I have to call to account a government that has been in power for 99 per cent of those last 20 years.
So, Mr. Speaker, there is ample justification for blaming the government for the lack of any industrial policy, and this is why it is difficult for Canada, an industrialized nation, to match many other countries at this point. So, here we are, Mr. Speaker, coming with band-aids to salvage what can be saved, and this is unfortunate. A genuine industrial strategy would have enabled a number of industries to stick it out. Those industries would have been forewarned. Union co-operation could have been obtained. The importance of what is called productivity could have been foreseen, to meet international competition. There has been no strategy, there has been no concern for the future, there has been a lack of foresight, although to govern means to be able to anticipate future developments. I submit we have every justification to blame the government for not establishing the industrial strategy that was of vital importance for Canada's future. They failed to do so, and today they resent our blaming the government's failure to create such an industrial strategy. Clearly the government must accept not a part of, but the total responsibility for the want of such a strategy, and therefore the responsibility for the growing misery in this country where Canadians are greatly concerned about the ability of their administrators.
This is the long and the short of it, Mr. Speaker. I doubt there is any government Member who is not embarrassed at having to defend the current economic conditions we are going through, because of the lack of a long-term strategy.
Mr. Speaker, this is not to say that the government must get involved daily in industry or the private affairs of individuals.
The duty of the state is to propose major trends and policies which will be of interest to the private sector, for example, incentives to invest in the country, and therefore it must be in a position to provide this additional assistance which is often required. And the state also has the power to steer those industries toward sensitive sectors and regions which the unemployment rate has made vulnerable. The state can do that, but without substituting for private companies. That is all we are asking for. But again that is part of a well-orchestrated industrial policy and strategy. I repeat-and I have said it before-the situation will remain unchanged until such time as the Government agrees to meet with union and industry spokesmen and spells out its mid- and long-term outlook. But that is not being done in the energy sector.
Everyone knows that investments of $40-odd million will be required because the Government undertook to substitute for private industries. That is what happened because the Government decided to substitute for private industries instead of giving them free rein to do what they can do better than the state. And the same is true in other areas. It has therefore become urgent to introduce an industrial strategy, and we would be remiss if we did not take the Government to task for failing to do anything about it during the past 20 years. As a result, thousands of Canadians are now deeply concerned. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did say that a hard winter is ahead of us, and other agencies have confirmed that the unemployment rate will remain at 12 per cent. Of course, nothing has been done to solve that problem.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion brags about the $1 billion recently earmarked by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for a number of new projects which will make it possible for thousands of Canadians to work for 20 or 26 weeks before going back to the unemployment insurance counters. That is not the way to build our country and give Canadians renewed confidence.
I could recite long lists of figures and talk about the huge bankruptcies we had in 1982; 40 per cent of those 8,074 bankruptcies occurred in my province. And God knows, Mr. Speaker, as you do, that the people of my province are worried as well about the lack of any industrial strategy which they deplore. So we are amply justified in blaming the Government today. I am quite certain that some Liberal members are also extremely disappointed because they were unable to influence the Cabinet which has refused to meet urgent needs and introduce that industrial strategy for the future of our country. We are now demanding it in stronger terms than ever. It has never been so urgent, but the harm has been done and the Government must assume full responsibility for that. With respect to the lack of industrial strategy, the Government will not get off the hook as easily as that, even though its advice is that we should forget the past.
How can anyone ask Canadians to have faith in this Government, responsible as it is for the mess we are in? That is impossible, Mr. Speaker. That is why of course we are again trying today to convince the Government to accept a proposal which has to be implemented, namely the introduction of an industrial strategy. I would hope that this time the government will realize its importance as a key solution for many years to come. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it is too late, much too late, and you cannot ask starving Canadians to tighten their belts further. But Canadians will certainly remember that the blame for this belt tightening is to be laid not on this side but on members on the other side who would take no heed of them. Although I still have a lot more to say, Mr. Speaker, I prefer to let other Hon. Members speak.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take this opportunity to discuss this matter with Hon. Members here in the house tonight, especially since I have not heard anyone on the other side of the House mention the hard facts, the real data on what we have done to establish science and technology here in Canada.

It is true that Canadian manufacturers, producers and exporters face incredible challenges. This is for a number of reasons. The inflation rate in Canada is not at the level we would like to see, nor is Canadian productivity as high as it should be by international comparison. Our international markets have gone soft as the world recession has taken a real hold. Other countries are suffering much more than we are because of these circumstances.
In this spirit of diminishing world markets, we see many countries resorting to non-tariff barriers and to a spate of other mechanisms designed to stop our exports, and we are an
Supply
exporting nation. The way to overcome these problems will not be easy. We have never pretended that it would be, but certainly the cutting edge of our economic strategy for the future must be the encouragement of technological research and development. It is through this approach that we will be able to compete in international markets in the days, years and decades ahead.
The paper released last year entitled, "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s" recognized the important contribution research and innovation has made in the past and will make in the future to economic growth. Its single most important message was that we must concentrate our efforts on various industries in Canada, including resource and industrial development, export promotion, transportation and communication infrastructure, and the development of manpower skills. A solid research base is fundamental to success in all these areas.
In January 1981 the federal Government committed itself to a major increase in the level of research and development, namely, that we would go up to 1.5 per cent of the gross national product by the year 1985. I believe the way we are doing this is the correct approach. Approximately 50 per cent of this increase will come from industry itself, one-third will come from the federal Government and the remaining one-sixth will come from a combination of provincial governments, universities and private institutions. This ambitious target is one which I believe we have to meet if we are to acquire the newly emerging technologies we need badly in order to create jobs in the country.
What progress have we made in less than two years since the program of 1.5 per cent of GNP devoted to research and development was entered into? One might argue that we have not gone far enough, but the results are most encouraging. In less than two years we have gone up from less than 0.9 per cent of gross national product to over 1.2 per cent. It shows what we can do when we have the collective will, when we set those targets and we set our priorities. This has been no mean accomplishment, particularly in the period of recession that we have faced.
Another thing that happened, which I think is significant, is that during this period we have attempted to achieve more research and development by a co-operative relationship between industry and government. In the first two years covered by the framework, the federal expenditures on research and development rose by nearly $435 million. The main estimates for 1982-1983 will increase R and D expenditures even further by an additional $250 million. It is important to note that this increase is going primarily to industrial research and development where it will have the best opportunity to create more jobs for Canadians. The R and D activities

November 15, 1982
Supply
financed by the federal Government but which are performed by industry will have almost doubled in three years.
Federal assistance to industry in support of research and innovation takes a number of forms. We are all familiar with the Industrial Research Assistance Program administered by the National Research Centre; the Enterprise Development Program and the Defence Industry Productivity Program. These are programs of the federal Government aimed at providing technological information services and creating new centres for advanced technology. We have developed two university innovation centres, and we are developing ten universities with the capability of doing electronic research right across this country in every one of our Provinces. In addition, we have used the federal procurement and contracting out policies to support increased R and D of Canadian industry. Twenty two per cent of the federal Government's 1982-1983 budget for research and development in the natural sciences is directly targeted to industry. All of these efforts and accomplishments to date, in spite of the tough economic times we face, are in addition to the tax incentives granted for innovation and development for new research.
As many Members in this House are probably aware, we have the 100 per cent write-off. In addition to that, we have an additional 50 per cent write-off for new research and development. On top of that, we have a generous tax credit, all of it aimed at increasing the ability of the private sector to go out and invest in new technology and do new research. When you take into consideration these tax incentives that are being offered, you find that they provide up to 80 cents on each dollar of new investment in research and development. That is a fairly generous program. In addition, we are undertaking discussions with the private sector to see if these approaches can be better honed, if they can be better developed, if there are new ways to channel more private sector funds in a more advantageous manner so they can flow into research and development. We have seen some innovations from the private sector, such as the scientific research investment certificate whereby investment firms have been able to raise money from people who might not otherwise be prepared to invest in science and in research and development. These innovations have come hand in hand with the programs that we have been introducing to try to encourage far greater research and development in Canada.
I mentioned that the approach we have been adopting has been one of co-operation between industry and government. I have outlined briefly a few of the Government programs. In terms of what industry itself has done, it has been one of the strongest contributors in the past and, of course, under our new program will be the strongest contributor, contributing at least half of the new expenditure on research and development. In terms of what industry has done, in 1979 industry's contribution to R and D rose 26 per cent. In 1980 it was 18 per cent. In 1981, it was 26 per cent, and for 1982 it is again estimated that it will reach 26 per cent. These are the highest rates of growth in research and development ever achieved in Canada.
One of the problems which I do not think has been completely documented, and I would not want to go overboard in making the case, is the whole role of foreign-controlled firms contributing to Canadian research and development. A study done in 1980 in terms of the electrical products industry indicated that while the foreign controlled firms enjoyed 65 per cent of the Canadian market, they contributed only 40 per cent of the research and development. I am not here to criticize foreign firms. I am here to say that I think every Canadian, every firm operating in Canada, whether Canadian-controlled or foreign-controlled, has an obligation to contribute to the future industrial strength of our country, to job creation, to the strengthening of Canada's capabilities and know-how by doing research here in Canada in fair proportion. By doing that in Canada and being able to export it we will as well be able to gain the royalties for selling the know-how. Research will feed upon itself. It is synergistic. The more you have, the more you will create, the better the atmosphere will be in Canada for creating the type of innovation we need. As I said, this will be the cutting edge of our new technological development.
We have had some tremendous examples of what can happen from this type of government and private sector cooperation when it comes to R and D. Northern Telecom is, I think, a signal example of what has happened in Canadian industry. It highlights the role of our high tech. I am pleased that Northern Telecom announced just recently that over the next five years it will spend an additional $1.2 billion on an R and D program in high technology digital communications systems. It estimated revenues from this new technology will be at least $13 billion, and it will create hundreds, even thousands of new jobs here in Canada. This is just one example of how Canadian industry, the Canadian private sector, has responded to this call we have put out for more R and D, is taking the risks and is working with Government, because people did come to Government to get assistance for these programs.
What we have accomplished is encouraging, and the Government is determined to use this solid basis to help develop technologies that we as Canadians need to adjust to changing world realities, the rapidly changing realities where in certain industries, such as computers, one seems to have a new generation coming out almost every year.
[ Translation]
However, Canada is facing a shortage of highly qualified scientific manpower in certain sectors. We now need practical experts who are capable of guiding and directing the new technologies that are being created in communications, information and biotechnology, while at the same time renewing our traditional resource-based industries.
Young people today are aware of these trends and more and more, they are opting for courses in applied science and commerce at our universities. The latter are starting to adapt their training programs to the demands of the eighties, but are
November 15, 1982

having to cope with financial constraints. Engineering, computer science and commerce departments are finding it difficult to recruit staff and are losing experienced teachers to the lure of higher salaries offered by the private sector. Furthermore, excellent labour market conditions for students with a bachelor's degree in fields where the demand is high prevent those students from doing graduate work. For instance, the Ministry of State for Science and Technology examined the outlook for engineering graduates and found that between 1979 and 1985, the demand for engineers would exceed the national supply. The shortage will be particularly acute at the postgraduate level. There will not be enough engineering specialists to fill teaching and research positions in industry, government and the universities. The ministry also found that industry was very concerned about the availability of highly qualified research staff and the problems that universities were experiencing in meeting demand. We are glad to see, however, that the industrial and commercial sectors are approaching this problem in a very constructive and innovative fashion.
Some industries are entering into co-operative agreements with the universities, which is another way of meeting their requirements for human resources. Similarly, during the past year, a number of companies have entered into direct aid agreements with universities in Canada. For instance, the Bank of Montreal is subsidizing studies on international finance, IBM is supporting marine sciences and Mitel and Systemhouse are encouraging studies on office automation.
The federal Government has recognized that Canada's supply of skilled human resources is critical to our technological development and has taken major steps to strengthen university research and training capacity in Canada.
I would like to summarize some of these measures that we have taken in recent years. First, the three federal research granting councils, the Medical Research Council, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, were reorganized to focus on training research manpower and maintaining a basic university research capacity in respective fields of study and on orienting more of their research support toward issues of national concern. These Councils have prepared five-year plans and have reassessed their programs in light of past experience and future priorities.
The Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council supports university research and research training in areas directly related to industrial growth. It has greatly expanded its highly qualified manpower programs by increasing the number and the value of graduate scholarships, providing longterm research associateships, both at the universities and in the private sector, and by establishing undergraduate summer research bursary programs so that more students can be attracted to postgraduate studies in the scientific and technological areas.
Supply
We also have direct federal support of university research and research training. It now totals $477 million. Since 1979 the budgets of the granting Councils have been increased by $170 million, or 75 per cent. These figures demonstrate our Government's commitment to doing something about research and development to manpower training in Canada.
The impact of these measures has indeed been encouraging. The strategic research grants are attracting some of the best researchers. We have seen the emergence of fibre optics, video techs, radio relay systems and many other products of the future through our co-operative programs. We stand in the forefront with the Canadarm and with satellites such as the one Canadians proudly saw launched, recently. Our domestic communication satellite system is the best in the world.
I understand that I am running out of time. I would not want to strain the indulgence of the House, which has always been courteous in the past. Perhaps I could ask for one more minute in order to get these important facts on the record.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I thank Hon. Members for their indulgence. These are areas where we have become world leaders in technological development. We have shown that we can do it.
Most important, the challenge in the days ahead is to ensure that we have not only technological development and manpower development but that the public and private sector, business, including those which are foreign controlled, labour, our universities and academics and governments at all levels, lock arms to increase further our ability to compete. This can be done by working together in our collective will and effort, our collective ability united in a consensus for action, a consensus for action based on new research and new ideas for the 1980s.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank Hon. Members for allowing me to participate in this debate, however short it might be. I was particularly interested to hear the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) because he made a statement which I believe is very appropriate to the remarks I wish to make this evening. He stated that research feeds on itself.
I would like to remind all Hon. Members that 15 years ago Great Canadian Oil Sands, 100 per cent owned by the Sun Oil Company of the United States, ventured into the tar sands in northeastern Alberta to conduct a giant research and development project. Today, that project produces 145,000 barrels of oil each and every day. This has contributed at least $20 billion to the Canadian balance of payments picture over the life of that one giant research project. It was not done, as the NDP says, with Government intervention. It was not accomplished by the Government saying that it will prop the company up if it tries to develop these oil sands. This was accomplished by foreign private enterprise, without one nickle of the Canadian taxpayers' money either at the provincial or federal level.
I remind Hon. Members of that fact. We heard the NDP Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) who said that what

November 15, 1982
Supply
the development strategy in Canada needs today is more Government regulations, more Government input, more Government control and more Government ownership. I simply want to ask how much more government the Canadian people must suffer before the Socialists realize the destruction they have wrought upon our country.
When I talk about Socialists, 1 am talking about the NDP who have propped up the Liberals during the 1970s. The NDP is saying that development strategy of the 1970s was not there. It was the New Democratic Party that propped up the present Government.
I would like to return to the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Willowdale who said that research feeds on itself. I would point out that from the original investment at the Sun plant of Great Canadian Oil Sands, which is now Suncor at Fort McMurray, a town of 30,000 people developed. From there, the next plant, Syncrude Canada, came on stream. Once again, this was a result of private investors with no Government subisidies, loans or guarantees. Mr. Speaker, the issue I want to address tonight is a good example of what I call government waste. It might not involve a very large amount of money, but the whole scenario is pretty wretched.
It was first drawn to my attention early last July by the editor of the Bridge River-Lillooet News, who received this package by courier; actually, on July 4 or July 5. This package was sent out by the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) and was to be in the hands of 576 community newspapers across Canada by or in advance of July 1 for use during the Dominion Day celebrations. This particular editor was incensed because it had come by courier and he wanted me to check into the matter. I therefore put a question on the order paper and asked what was the purpose of the package and what it contained. The answer was that the package contained a photograph of the Minister of State for Mines and the Governor General of Canada. There was also a "Canada Then and Now" map package and a news release from the Minister's office for use in conjunction with Dominion Day. It was distributed by Prestige Mailing Systems Limited and sent by courier service to 576 members of the Canadian Community Newspaper Association. As I said, this package was supposed to have arrived in advance of July 1.
1 then asked, whether any packages were mailed through Canada Post Corporation and, if not, for what reason, and the answer was, "No". Technical problems with printing and packing the maps had resulted in an unforeseen delay of the availability date for mailing the package. Therefore, courier service was utilized in order that the package would reach recipients as close to Dominion Day as possible. These packages were sent out on June 30. There was no possible way they could reach their destinations by July 1.
I then asked what the cost of production of the package was and the total cost of delivery. The answer was that the cost of producing these 576 packages amounted to $1,783 and the cost of the courier service was close to $6,000. This cost of production bears some scrutiny because we found out that the three maps alone contained in the package itself sell for $5.95. We thought that because there were 576 maps, perhaps the Government might have received a discount on the bulk sale. That was not the case, sir. We telephoned the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Canada Map Office, and were informed that there was no discount given and that they cost $5.95 per package. If one multiplies this amount by the 576 sent out, one arrives at a figure of $3,427. We therefore see a discrepancy of $1,650 just in the production of the package.
November 15, 1982

If that were not bad enough, even though these packages were put into shape too late to be sent out to arrive at their destinations by July 1, a courier service was employed and $6,000 was spent to get these packages to their destinations. All of them arrived too late for their purpose.
When I asked the Minister of State for Mines last week whether she could justify this expense, she said that the cost of distribution was completely justified in the national interest. What kind of national interest is served by a clear waste of $6,000? I would ask for a more complete answer. I would like to have the whole situation explained to me and to the taxpayers. I hope the Auditor General will consider the matter at some point.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, responding to the Elon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway), I must say that his concern is one which ought to be placed before Parliament. Perhaps, as he said in his closing remarks, it ought to be reviewed by the Auditor General and we should have the pleasure of his comments at some point in time so that we can pursue the debate even further. However, let me just say a few words with regard to the national atlas of Canada to which the maps in question belong.
Canada has had a national atlas since 1906 and five editions have been produced over 75 years under both Liberal and Conservative governments. Granted, the Conservative government was only short-lived. These atlases contain maps which reflect and summarize our national resources, growth and achievement. They parallel the evolution of Canada since almost the beginning of this century. The lastest Fifth edition is especially significant this year. It portrays Canada as we were in 1867, the complex evolution of our lands and territories and the make-up of the modern nation.
The medium of maps is a very effective way in which to inform Canadians about national development and to celebrate our progress as a nation since Confederation in this our constitutional year. For this reason, it was appropriate to make the maps available as near as possible to Canada Week.
Furthermore, while it is usually not very difficult for large newspapers and the major media organizations to obtain rapid access and awareness of new publications, that is not always so easy for the hundreds of relatively smaller weekly newspapers in this country. These grassroots community papers are read by many Canadians outside the major cities and they were our target group in this particular mail-out.
Technical difficulties in completing the maps reduced the time available for distribution by Canada Post. Courier service was chosen in order to ensure delivery as reasonably close as possible to Canada Week. The first Canadian to receive a copy of the maps was His Excellency the Governor General of Canada, and rightly so. A photograph of this presentation was provided with the package of maps for possible use by recipient newspapers thus informing their readers of the existence of the maps. The approximate cost of this was $3,000.
Adjournment Debate
In view of the significance of the subject matter of the maps and our wish to let all Canadians know about them, this was very low-cost advertising in the marketing of these national maps.

ENERGY-COLD LAKE PROJECT-LOAN MADE TO IMPERIAL OIL. NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 30 I rose in the House and asked the then minister of energy, mines and resources the state of the $40 million loan to Imperial Oil in an attempt to salvage the Cold Lake project. The Minister did advise the House that the loan was lost forever, that the loan would not have to be repaid on July 1 because there was the agreement in place that if the project did not proceed at Cold Lake by July 1, 1982 these funds would be lost forever.
I then asked the Minister if he did not now recognize that the most destructive piece of legislation to hit Canada in a number of years was the National Energy Program, that it was the single instrument that was deterring investment in Canada, particularly in the oil and gas sector. The Minister totally ignored that question; he did not answer.
I would like to point out something to the Parliamentary Secretary who has been chosen to answer this question. The investment in Alsands and the Cold Lake Project in northeastern Alberta, both giant research and development projects, particularly the one in Cold Lake where the very first commercial in situ extraction was to take place, was approximately $10 billion, producing 140,000 barrels of oil a day. That would contribute approximately $2 billion a year or more to Canada's balance of payments. Over 25 years it would have produced 1.3 to 1.5 billion barrels of oil and would have employed, at peak construction, 10,000 people. Ongoing employment for the life of the project would have been between 3,000 and 4,000 people; indirect employment would have been approximately 6,500 people; total engineering manhours would have been approximately 50 million. Those figures apply to the one project only, the project at Cold Lake. Having regard to Alsands, which went down the tube, you could double all those figures. The amount of money to have been spent on facilities, which would have tremendous impact on the Canadian economy, was $9 billion for one plant; on facilities, $1 billion; infrastructure, another $1 billion; sustaining investment for the life of the project, $20 billion; operating expenses for the one project, and I am talking about Cold Lake, over its 25-year life, approximately $60 billion. This is a total of $90 billion of a direct investment into the economy of Canada at a time when jobs are needed and when the engines of the economy are winding down.
If you use the normal multiplier to determine the injection into the Canadian economy over that 25-year period, we would be looking at $250 billion to $350 billion as a result of the investment in that one plant at Cold Lake in northeastern Alberta. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker; $500 billion to $700

November 15, 1982
Adjournment Debate
billion if two plants, the Alsands and the Cold Lake, were allowed to proceed.
Why did they not proceed? We talk about research and development. The Alsands consortium and Imperial Oil at Cold Lake were ready to proceed. Because of the lack of foresight on the part of this Government, which would rather import oil from offshore, we lost $2 billion a year per plant. That represents a drain on our balance or payments. This money has to come from somewhere. When you drain off money for the purchase of off-shore oil, you affect interest rates and the money markets, and you hit jobs in Canada. I am not talking of just jobs created in northeastern Alberta, or in one province, I am talking about jobs in the steel industry, the automotive industry-jobs clear across this country. It was estimated that not one province would fail to benefit from the development of the Cold Lake project. Not one province would fail to benefit from the development of the Alsands project.
Eighteen months ago, Mr. Speaker, a number of Members of Parliament visited the Cold Lake and Alsands plants. The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), who will be replying to this question tonight, was with us. We toured those plants. He saw the vast investment and vast potential for Canada's energy scurity. He saw the vast potential for investment in the supply of pumps, steel and manpower from right across the country. He knows, if anyone knows, exactly what I am talking about.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I normally enjoy listening to the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), but I must say that tonight he has gone a bit overboard. It is correct to say that I was with him in his constituency at Fort McMurray and visited a number of the sites he referred to, but he forgets to mention in his remarks that the reason or reasons why the Alsands consortium decided against going ahead with the project was because of the economic realities of the time.
The Government of Canada and the Government of Alberta made a very, very strong proposal to the Alsands consortium; two levels of Government, Mr. Speaker, and it was the Alsands consortium decision alone not to proceed. When the Hon. Member stands in this House and points his finger at the Government of Canada, that is complete gobblydegook on his part. Those are the facts, and he ought to know better. To perpetrate that kind of thing on the Canadian people I think is intellectually dishonest.
I should remind the Hon. Member of the nature of the agreement effective February 1, 1981, whereby Imperial Oil Limited received advances to a maximum of $40 million to maintain the Cold Lake project. It was agreed that if, before the repayment date, the board of directors of Imperial Oil had passed a resolution suspending or cancelling the Cold Lake project, Imperial Oil would have no obligation to repay the amount borrowed. The effective date in this case was the latter of July 1, 1982, or the first anniversary of the full payment
date. In fact, the project was suspended before July 1, 1982 and consequently the obligation for repayment was removed.
As the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources noted when the matter of the Cold Lake project was discussed on July 30, 1982, Mr. Speaker, the period during which the Cold Lake project operated on the basis of the $40 million advance was a productive one, during which further engineering information was developed and employment was provided for a number of people in the Cold Lake region.
The Hon. Member for Athabasca notes that these two projects did not go ahead. I remind him that other projects in other countries have not gone ahead for the same economic reasons, that of world recession. Those are the reasons, Mr. Speaker, and those are the facts which the Hon. Member refuses to acknowledge and to place before this House. In fact, Mr. Speaker, his idol, his mentor, the Premier of the province of Alberta, has stated explicitly on a number of occasions that people ought not to be using 1980 as the benchmark for reference to oil and gas activity. But somehow the Hon. Member refuses, intentionally or otherwise, to recognize the facts of a world recession which has played havoc with these projects and many others, not only in Canada but in the U.S. as well as in European countries.

subtopic: ENERGY-INQUIRY RESPECTING PROGRAM CUTBACKS. (B) CHIP AND OFF-OIL PROGRAMS
ENERGY-INQUIRY RESPECTING PROGRAM CUTBACKS. (B) CHIP AND OFF-OIL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to pursue a question which I raised with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on his economic statement. The economic statement said that $616 million would be freed in the energy area by scaling back funds allocated to a number of programs, although he did not mention any specifically. He did, however, state that allocations for the Petroleum Incentives Program would remain at their existing levels.
If the economic statement were really serious about job creation, it would have delineated which projects were to be cut, at what loss of jobs, and for what gain in jobs in the new program, which is clearly a job creation program. Any reallocation of funds must mean a net increase in jobs. Nevertheless, nothing was specified.
Rumour has it that the CHIP program and Off Oil Program were again considered for cuts, and I asked about these. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) gave a wholly unsatisfactory reply, not giving assurances that they would not be. What is happening, it seems to me, is that we are seeing a further erosion of the valuable parts of the National Energy Program. We are losing the energy self-sufficiency and job creating aspects of the Program, while the give-aways to the corporations are continuing. I believe this is a sorely mistaken sense of priority.
First of all, let us consider the question of conservation. It is still true that conservation is the cheapest source of new energy and that it provides the most jobs. A study by the Economic
November 15, 1982

Council of Canada estimates that adding insulation to one million existing homes would produce 27,000 person years of employment, at a cost of 7,000 person years in the oil industry or, in other words, a net gain of 20,000 person years in jobs. Estimates are that it cost nearly $1 million to create a job in the tar sands, as an extreme example, while it costs $50,000 to $100,000 in conservation or the renewables. Further, the jobs are created where they are needed; that is, where people are living. They do not require the disruption of families or starting up new, single industry towns in trailer parks. Conservation programs minimize environmental destruction. Fixing up old houses where people already live is greatly to be preferred to disrupting native communities and risking serious environmental destruction by oil spills, for which we have as yet no technological solution.
It is true that there are problems in existing CHIP programs, quite apart from the urea formaldehyde scandal. There have been abuses, as the Government was warned. It was urged to establish proper inspection procedures. The answer now is not to abandon that Program but to correct the flaw in it and to institute proper inspection procedures.
The National Energy Program, as originally set out, had some laudable principles; self-sufficiency in energy and a move to conservation and the renewables being most notable amongst them. There was a recognition of the basic facts of life in energy, that we could not achieve self-sufficiency in Canada without substantial reliance on the renewables and conservation. But what happened then, Mr. Speaker? The highminded principles were relegated to the low budget area of the Program.
Petroleum Incentives Program grants are measured in the billions, but conservation is measured in the millions. What is wrong with the Petroleum Incentives Program grants? They are give-aways to corporations which pay no taxes, or less than their fair share. They mean that the public pays for exploration and gets no equity for it, while the companies talk about risk taking. They deplete the heritage which we have been given and which we have some obligation to pass on to future generations. Petroleum Incentives Program grants mean that expensive oil will be pursued, dug out and sent south at enormous cost in money and in social terms. People will pump more gas into their gas guzzlers and let heat seep out of their non-airtight houses. The Petroleum Incentives Program grants are a slow route to Canadianization. More fundamentally, they do not address our need for long-term energy security. They are directed at a non-renewable resource and, at best, postpone the day of reckoning. Eventually, and not all that far aheard, we are going to have to switch to renewable resources. The less we use now of the non-renewables, the easier it will to be make the switch.
The Petroleum Incentives Program is also inflationary, a factor that should count nowadays. It means pursuing ever more expensive forms of energy. The same money invested in conservation measures means savings in the here and now and in the long run, for with conservation you save year after year after year. Conservation means finding cheap oil again, the
Adjournment Debate
equivalent of oil at $5, $10 or $20 a barrel, depending on the particular measures used. That is far less than the oil that the Petroleum Incentives Program grants are directed toward.
Conservation and the renewables happen to be matters in which we can have our cake and eat it too. We can pursue a number of worthy objectives at the same time, instead of having to play one off against the other. We can create far more jobs than would be created from conventional nonrenewables. We can promote environmental protection instead of risking serious damage. We can respect native concerns and give them time to develop their priorities instead of imposing ours, from the south. We can maintain our standard of living, for alternative energy resources are rich and the technology is available. The lack has been in implementation, not in knowledge of what needs to be done. That is where the serious gap is. Meanwhile, we subsidize conventional energy sources and make the new ones "pay their own way", as they say, and make them compete unfairly.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources referred to maintaining the CHIP and off-oil programs, and wanting to use them more efficiently. Naturally I would want to commend him for any greater efficiency he can manage, but 1 would like to hear more. What does he mean by cutting? Does he mean to cut those, and if he does not cut those two particular programs, which programs will he cut?
Finally, I would like to challenge the Government to consider the real potential of the National Energy Program, especially its job-creation aspects. If it did the necessary calculations and took a critical look, I think it would find that its priorities would be reversed.

subtopic: ENERGY-INQUIRY RESPECTING PROGRAM CUTBACKS. (B) CHIP AND OFF-OIL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of the question and of the comments of the Hon. Member is not only of concern to her Party but to my Party as well.
Let me state quite clearly that the Government of Canada has no plans to abandon the Canadian Home Insulation Program and the Canada Oil Substitution Program. On the contrary, the Government is looking forward to maintaining strong support for energy conservation and substitution in the residential sector.
With respect to the Canada Oil Substitution Program, it is heartening to note that off-oil conversion activity has continued rather strongly during 1982, at a time when generally consumer spending is weak. Conversions from oil to electricity and renewable energy sources are on target. Conversions to natural gas are below target, as they were last year. From the time the Canada Oil Substitution Program was launched late in 1980 to the end of September 1982, it paid approximately 270,000 grants for a total of $ 183 million.
On the subject of CHIP, there existed some concern that the Program was not as effective as it might have been in helping to achieve potential saving available from home energy conser-

November 15, 1982
Adjournment Debate
vation. A large part of the problem appeared to lie in the structure of the CHIP grant which had the effect of encouraging some inflated prices and some questionable sales techniques, such as the marketing of attic and weatherstripping "specials" priced at or near the amount of the CHIP grant. To ameliorate the sitution, on November 9 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) announced changes in the grant formula and criteria of CHIP. These changes are intended to achieve more effective conservation activity and contribute toward the energy budget savings announced on October 27 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde).
Briefly, the changes to CHIP include that a home owner doing his own insulation work would obtain a CHIP grant on
60 per cent of the insulation materials, up to a maximum of $500. Originally, CHIP provided 100 per cent of material costs and 33.33 per cent of labour costs. Second, for work done by a contractor, 60 per cent of the contractor's bill would earn a CHIP grant, up to a maximum of $500. However, the home owner will be required to file a copy of the contractor's billing, showing a breakdown on labour and material costs so that the several costs could be checked by CHIP administrators against acceptable standards.
